family_judgments.evidence: The cloze elicits a fragment, the dialogue permits unconstrained lexical alternatives and is invalidly keyed, the MCQ measures recognition, and the transformation provides the target order. These yield materially unequal evidence for the same operations.

The transformation effectively changes polar-question formation into arranging/copying a supplied sequence, while the MCQ changes production into option recognition; these response mechanisms weaken the declared KC evidence differently.
All formats concern offering to close the open window, but only the dialogue leaves the lexical action open enough for the reasonable “shut” alternative.

criteria.evidence: Producing “Shall I close” in the fixed frame requires SHALL plus a base-form complement and operator-before-subject order.
The supplied frame fixes the object and requires no substantial grammatical operation beyond the declared modal and polar-question construction.
The response blank precedes “the window?”, so a successful response must supply both SHALL and the inverted subject-operator sequence.
The instruction explicitly requires “shall” and “close”, and the fixed continuation makes “Shall I close” the determinate grammatical completion.
The keyed response covers the required constrained completion; no solver-proposed unkeyed alternative was supplied.
Success also depends on parsing the fixed noun phrase “the window,” but this is low lexical burden at B2.
A valid offer with SHALL requires the declared modal and polar-question form, as in “Shall I close the window?”
The dialogue’s required response does not impose another major grammatical construction beyond the declared target.
The instruction requires an offer using SHALL, so a response cannot receive credit through a non-SHALL offer such as “I can close it.”
The open dialogue permits multiple natural SHALL offers about the window; the solver-proposed “Shall I shut the window?” is linguistically and contextually reasonable.
“Shall I shut the window?” is a reasonable unkeyed response under the instruction, but the accepted set contains only “Shall I close the window?” Its rejection makes the item invalid as scored.
The open response adds lexical-choice burden (close versus shut) and pragmatic wording burden that are not declared KCs.
The keyed option uniquely combines SHALL, a base-form complement, and finite-operator inversion; each distractor targets a stated defect.
The alternatives do not require a major undeclared construction to identify the target.
A learner may select A by eliminating visibly anomalous forms, especially “Do I shall...”, rather than independently constructing the target; this is recognition-format cueing, not a different KC.
Only A is a grammatical, contextually appropriate SHALL offer among the presented options.
Single-choice scoring correctly keys the only defensible option; no solver-proposed unkeyed alternative exists.
Option-elimination and sensitivity to deliberately implausible distractors create test-taking burden beyond the target operations.
The required output realizes both KCs, but the cue already supplies the target word order “shall / I / close,” reducing evidence that the learner can independently form inversion.
The requested response needs no major undeclared grammar beyond the modal polar question.
The ordered cue allows copying the target sequence and adding a question mark, so success can partly bypass independently selecting/inverting the finite operator.
Using all cue words with no added content determines “Shall I close the window?”
The tightly constrained cue supports the sole accepted response; no reasonable unkeyed solver alternative was proposed.
The learner must also reinterpret the source statement and adopt Maya’s first-person perspective, a task-format burden not represented in the Q-row.

summary: Rejected: the dialogue rejects a reasonable unkeyed SHALL offer, and format differences provide unequal and sometimes shortcut-based evidence for the declared KCs.
